material.advice: This material is dense with long sentences and technical terms (e.g., 'dynamic attractor states', 'respiratory sinus arrhythmia'). Break each chunk into smaller breath groups, especially chunks 13, 19, and 35. Use the hint keywords as memory anchors, and practice recalling the logical flow from one chunk to the next. Pay attention to parallel structures like 'The ability to...' in chunk 1 and the step-by-step lists in chunks 18 and 24.

chunks.text: So much of life, the ability to learn and lean into just enough stress that you trigger learning. The ability to listen when you want to react. The ability to force yourself to get up and work on the book or the thing that you don't want to do. So much of that is top-down influences.
chunks.translation: 生活中很大一部分，在于学习的能力，以及投入恰到好处的压力以触发学习。在于想反应时却能倾听的能力。在于强迫自己起床，去写那本书或做你不想做的事情的能力。这其中很大一部分是自上而下的影响。

chunks.text: Focus is obviously in a tunnel, but then how much alertness? I don't think anyone's ever described it before, but when you look at levels of arousal in a game like Hot Hands and believe it or not, there are some equivalent data on this or data on the equivalent sort of thing.
chunks.translation: 专注显然是在一个隧道里，但警觉度要多少呢？我认为之前没有人描述过这一点，但当你观察像“热手”这样的游戏中的唤醒水平时，信不信由你，有一些关于这方面的等效数据，或者关于等效事物的数据。

chunks.text: When you're waiting for a time trial and you're waiting for something to happen and you have to react quickly, that's the state of mind you want to be in to learn something that's hard for you, but beneficial for you. Period, end of story. So hopefully that'll help people kind of find that mental groove.
chunks.translation: 当你在等待计时赛，等待某事发生，并且必须快速反应时，那就是你想要的学习状态，去学习对你来说困难但有益的东西。就这样，故事结束。所以希望这能帮助人们找到那种心理状态。

chunks.text: And then as you learn, if you find you're getting too stressed, that doesn't that brings down reaction time. It actually you you start making false positive. You start moving your hands away before the person even does anything. Okay. Hopefully that will help people understand the level of attention and why it's so tiring after about 90 minutes. And you're like, "Okay, I need to take a break."
chunks.translation: 然后随着你学习，如果你发现自己压力太大，那不会——那会降低反应时间。实际上你会开始做出假阳性反应。你开始在对方甚至还没做任何事之前就把手移开。好吧。希望这能帮助人们理解注意力的水平，以及为什么大约90分钟后会如此疲惫。你会想，“好吧，我需要休息一下。”

chunks.text: Step back and acknowledge there's a lot out there about how to get through trauma. But what are the unifying themes and can I put a structure on those themes that helps people navigate all of that? What's the business of >> >> having a great life? So we talk about that.
chunks.translation: 退后一步，承认有很多关于如何度过创伤的信息。但统一的主题是什么？我能否在这些主题上建立一个结构，帮助人们驾驭所有这些？拥有美好生活的要务是什么？所以我们谈论那个。

chunks.text: We hear be present. There's this massive study out of Harvard a few years ago that a wandering mind is an unhappy mind. I'm sure you're familiar with the data. You ping people throughout the day, you ask them what they're doing and how present they are to it. Turns out happiness is really about being present, having your attention what's called present tethered awareness.
chunks.translation: 我们听到要活在当下。几年前哈佛有一项大规模研究，表明走神是不快乐的心灵。我相信你熟悉这些数据。你全天候地询问人们，问他们在做什么以及他们有多投入。结果表明幸福真的在于活在当下，让你的注意力成为所谓的“当下系留意识”。

chunks.text: You're focused on what's happening now, even if it's unpleasant. People report that as being much happier on average than if their mind is someplace else. Daydreaming has its place, but daydreaming is usually mind wandering to bad things, things of past, things of future, we're just not present. The converse is also true that focusing on what you're doing is a great way to build up your mental health.
chunks.translation: 你专注于现在发生的事情，即使它不愉快。人们报告说，平均而言，这比心思在别处要快乐得多。白日梦有其位置，但白日梦通常是思绪游荡到坏事、过去的事、未来的事，我们就是不在当下。反过来也成立：专注于你正在做的事情是建立心理健康的绝佳方式。

chunks.text: So then I started asking cuz I'm a biologist not a psychologist, what is presence? Does it mean um anchoring my visual attention? What How do I be present? Cuz otherwise it's just a bumper sticker.
chunks.translation: 所以然后我开始问，因为我是生物学家不是心理学家，什么是临在？它是否意味着锚定我的视觉注意力？我如何临在？因为否则它只是一个保险杠贴纸。

chunks.text: And otherwise I look I love psychologist said these beautiful studies that discover phenomena, but then it's like if you're going to say like fall asleep, what is falling asleep? And we can talk about that. What is being present? Okay. So be here now, I think Ram Dass said that. Great, be here now. How? How do we move our brain from thinking about the future and the past to what's happening now?
chunks.translation: 否则我看起来——我喜欢心理学家说的这些发现现象的精美研究，但然后就像如果你要说入睡，什么是入睡？我们可以谈论那个。什么是临在？好吧。所以“此时此地”，我想是拉姆·达斯说的。很好，此时此地。如何？我们如何让大脑从思考未来和过去转移到现在正在发生的事情？

chunks.text: Okay, so that means perceptions about what's only in our immediate physical environment. It means not thinking, not doing, not planning, but asking questions about the immediate physical environment. So we can do this just right now and you can do this anytime you want to be more present.
chunks.translation: 好的，所以这意味着感知只存在于我们 immediate 物理环境中的东西。这意味着不思考、不做、不计划，而是询问关于 immediate 物理环境的问题。所以我们现在就可以这样做，你可以在任何时候想要更临在时这样做。

chunks.text: And I want to just preface this by saying what I'm about to describe is not the end point. It's the way to get into the present. But what you do next is critically important too. So first, you ask trivial questions about your immediate environment that can only be answered accurately by focusing on the present.
chunks.translation: 我想先说明，我即将描述的不是终点。它是进入当下的方法。但你接下来做什么也至关重要。所以首先，你问一些关于你 immediate 环境的琐碎问题，这些问题只有通过专注于当下才能准确回答。

chunks.text: So for instance, bring our mind toward obviously >> >> perception of the present. Duh, there's nothing, you know, profound about that. But it's what they take our mind away from >> >> that's critically important.
chunks.translation: 例如，将我们的心智转向显然 >> >> 对当下的感知。废话，你知道，那没什么深奥的。但正是它们让我们的心智远离 >> >> 那才是至关重要的。

chunks.text: The brain, there's a whole section on thinking, what is thinking? The brain works in what are called dynamic attractor states, which is nerd speak for if I take a ball bearing and I put it on a on a plate, it essentially can move in any direction. There's some details related to the smoothness of the bearing and the plate, etc. But if I put a little groove on that plate and I tilt the plate slightly, it obviously will go toward the groove. It'll get into the groove. And then, if I turn that groove into a I make it more concave and eventually a trench, the ball bearing stays there. That's how your brain works.
chunks.translation: 大脑，有一整节关于思考，什么是思考？大脑以所谓的动态吸引子状态运作，这是书呆子话，意思是如果我拿一个滚珠轴承放在盘子上，它基本上可以向任何方向移动。有一些关于轴承和盘子光滑度等的细节。但如果我在盘子上刻一个小槽，并稍微倾斜盘子，它显然会向槽移动。它会进入槽中。然后，如果我把那个槽变成一个更凹的，最终变成沟槽，滚珠轴承就留在那里。你的大脑就是这样运作的。

chunks.text: The more that you seed a thought, the more that you seed a perception, the more that brain circuits are devoted to things related to that thought or perception. So, when you want to be present, something that we know from excellent data a this large study at at Harvard, but subsequent studies as well, is so critical for happiness, the way to practice that is to learn from taking your mind from thinking and doing and remembering about things of past and future to just anchoring your perception to the present.
chunks.translation: 你越是播种一个想法，越是播种一个感知，就有越多的脑回路专门用于与那个想法或感知相关的事物。所以，当你想临在时，我们从哈佛的这项大型研究以及后续研究中获得的优秀数据知道，这对幸福如此关键，练习的方法是学会将你的心智从思考、行动和回忆过去与未来的事情，转变为仅仅将你的感知锚定在当下。

chunks.text: It doesn't require meditating. Meditation is one form of that. What are What are we doing when we meditate? We close our eyes, we focus on our breathing, that's here now, and we focus on quote unquote third eye center or whatever, but that's actually interoception. It's focusing on our internal bodily state, which is not that great, frankly, if you look at the data, for being present in a happy way.
chunks.translation: 它不需要冥想。冥想是其中一种形式。当我们冥想时我们在做什么？我们闭上眼睛，专注于呼吸，那是此时此地，我们专注于所谓的第三眼中心或其他什么，但那实际上是内感受。它是专注于我们内部身体状态，坦率地说，如果你看数据，对于以快乐的方式临在来说，那并不是那么好。

chunks.text: Most people who are overly focused on their internal state in the present are like, my heart rate is increasing. My heart rate's too low. I'm sweating. I'm uncomfortable. You start thinking about the fact that like your your you know, your boxers are like pulled up on one one leg, you know, they That's not the way to get present and calm and aware.
chunks.translation: 大多数过度关注当下内部状态的人会想，我的心率在增加。我的心率太低了。我在出汗。我不舒服。你开始思考这样的事实：你的，你知道，你的平角裤一条腿往上缩了，你知道，它们——那不是变得临在、平静和觉察的方式。

chunks.text: The way to get present, calm, and aware and be able to move forward from that in a in the best way is to ask questions about your immediate physical environment. Once you do that, remember that's just the first step. The second step is to use that heightened level of awareness to ask yourself, "What do I want to What do I actually want to do next? What do I want to say next? What do I want to think about next?" This is the way that you take control of your thoughts.
chunks.translation: 变得临在、平静和觉察，并能够以最佳方式向前迈进的方法是，询问关于你 immediate 物理环境的问题。一旦你这样做，记住那只是第一步。第二步是利用那种提高的觉察水平问自己，“我想要——我实际上接下来想做什么？我接下来想说什么？我接下来想思考什么？”这就是你控制思想的方式。

chunks.text: Here are the steps to learning. You need to focus, obviously, to learn. To focus, you need to be alert. To get alert, there are many things you can do, and I talk about all of them in the book. There are foundational things like sleep, all right, that's going to help you get alert and focused, but there are also things like exercise.
chunks.translation: 以下是学习的步骤。显然，你需要专注才能学习。要专注，你需要警觉。要变得警觉，你可以做很多事情，我在书中谈到了所有方法。有一些基础的事情，比如睡眠，好吧，那会帮助你变得警觉和专注，但也有一些事情，比如锻炼。

chunks.text: We all hear that exercise makes our brain better, it makes us better at learning. Exercise makes you better at learning for two reasons. One, it increases the catecholamines, dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine. So, so in the 4 to 6 hours after exercise, you are more alert and you can focus better, unless you exercise to exhaustion.
chunks.translation: 我们都听说锻炼使大脑更好，使我们更善于学习。锻炼使你更善于学习有两个原因。第一，它增加儿茶酚胺、多巴胺、肾上腺素和去甲肾上腺素。所以，在锻炼后的4到6小时内，你更警觉，能更好地集中注意力，除非你锻炼到筋疲力尽。

chunks.text: If you have leg day for, you know, you 10 sets of 10 and on the squats followed by a bunch of hamstring work and etc., your brain's not going to be so good at focusing, but, you know, 45 to 75 minutes of hard training, not taken to extreme, a bit like what we did this morning, that was a little bit on the lighter side, not just because we didn't have a whole lot of time, but you're going to come out of that more alert because you have more adrenaline in your body, >> >> more norepinephrine being released in your brain, and more dopamine being released in your brain, and dopamine is a critical component for learning, okay?
chunks.translation: 如果你有练腿日，你知道，10组10次的深蹲，接着一堆腘绳肌训练等等，你的大脑不会那么擅长集中注意力，但是，你知道，45到75分钟的艰苦训练，不做到极端，有点像我们今天早上做的，那有点偏轻，不仅因为我们没有很多时间，但你会从中出来更警觉，因为你体内有更多肾上腺素，>> >> 大脑释放更多去甲肾上腺素，大脑释放更多多巴胺，而多巴胺是学习的关键组成部分，好吗？

chunks.text: Focus then becomes easier to access. And in your focus, what are you focusing on? You need to focus on making errors through genuine attempts to do something, something physical, maybe a tennis serve, or you're learning billiards, something cognitive, you're trying to learn a language. The error between what you can currently do and what you're trying to do, the error, is the signal that the neurons, the nerve cells, need to change.
chunks.translation: 然后专注变得更容易进入。而在你的专注中，你专注于什么？你需要专注于通过真诚尝试做某事来犯错，一些身体的事情，也许是网球发球，或者你在学台球，一些认知的事情，你在尝试学习一门语言。你目前能做的和你试图做的之间的误差，那个误差，是神经元、神经细胞需要改变的信号。

chunks.text: It runs through a circuit involving the cerebellum and a bunch of other things, but that gap is what the brain tries to close. If you can do something, there's no reason for your brain to change. And the agitation you feel from those errors reflects elevated levels of epinephrine and norepinephrine in the body and brain, respectively.
chunks.translation: 它通过一个涉及小脑和一堆其他东西的回路运行，但那个差距是大脑试图关闭的。如果你能做某事，你的大脑就没有理由改变。你从那些错误中感受到的激动反映了身体和大脑中分别升高的肾上腺素和去甲肾上腺素水平。

chunks.text: And those tag literally chemically tag the synapses. I mean, there's some additional steps, but they tag those synapses so that then at night when you sleep, the synapses rearrange and you close the gap between your current ability and the ability you're striving to achieve. That's how it works.
chunks.translation: 那些标记字面上化学标记突触。我的意思是，有一些额外的步骤，但它们标记那些突触，以便然后在晚上你睡觉时，突触重新排列，你关闭当前能力和你努力达到的能力之间的差距。这就是它的运作方式。

chunks.text: So, a curiosity and willingness to learn gets you to the gate of learning. The making of errors through genuine attempts puts the key in and turns the key. The agitation is walking through that gate and then getting some sleep or maybe even uh you know, a day or two later even if you don't sleep quite as well as you would like, just some time for the synapses to rearrange, that's the last piece.
chunks.translation: 所以，好奇心和学习的意愿让你来到学习的大门前。通过真诚尝试犯错将钥匙插入并转动钥匙。激动是走过那扇门，然后睡一觉，或者甚至呃你知道，一两天后，即使你睡得不如你希望的那么好，只是给突触一些时间重新排列，那是最后一块。

chunks.text: There's an additional piece that can reinforce it all, which is self-testing. If you want to get good at something and stay good at it and continue to get better at it, you need to self-test. Mental self-testing is the best way to consolidate learning and learn faster. What do I mean by that? I don't mean visualization.
chunks.translation: 还有一个额外的部分可以强化这一切，那就是自我测试。如果你想擅长某事并保持擅长并继续变得更好，你需要自我测试。心理自我测试是巩固学习和更快学习的最佳方式。我是什么意思？我不是指可视化。

chunks.text: I mean, asking yourself like for me, if I wanted make my memory better, generally speaking, I might think, "Okay, so that was uh September 11th, 2001. Where was I exactly? What were some of the details?" Now, that might be a something I might not want to think about, but if I were to say, "Okay, I'm going to go back to my um you know, year one neuroscience >> >> graduate school training."
chunks.translation: 我的意思是，问自己，比如对我来说，如果我想让我的记忆力更好，一般来说，我可能会想，“好吧，那是2001年9月11日。我到底在哪里？有哪些细节？”现在，那可能是我可能不想思考的事情，但如果我说，“好吧，我要回到我的嗯你知道，第一年神经科学 >> >> 研究生训练。”

chunks.text: Of course, I already know what a synapse is, I know what neurons are, I know what astrocytes are. I know all this stuff. It's embedded so deeply in me, I can almost do it in my sleep. But then I think, "Yeah, that's right. Like, what is the role of astrocytes in this?" And I go, "Okay." Cuz that's stuff that's relevant to me. When you hit the point where you can't remember something, you go and look it up. Boom, you've now closed that gap again and it reinforces those synapses that were weakening. Yeah.
chunks.translation: 当然，我已经知道什么是突触，我知道神经元是什么，我知道星形胶质细胞是什么。我知道所有这些东西。它如此深深地嵌入我，我几乎可以在睡梦中做到。但然后我想，“是的，没错。比如，星形胶质细胞在其中的作用是什么？”然后我说，“好吧。”因为那是对我有用的东西。当你到达记不住某事的地步时，你去查一下。砰，你现在再次关闭了那个差距，它强化了那些正在减弱的突触。是的。

chunks.text: So, if you're trying to learn something new or you want to get maintain information from way back when, you need to retest. So, that's how you learn. You have to bring yourself to those points of agitation. I wish I'd learned that in the third grade. I wish they had told me that.
chunks.translation: 所以，如果你试图学习新东西，或者你想保持很久以前的信息，你需要重新测试。所以，那就是你学习的方式。你必须把自己带到那些激动的点。我希望我在三年级就学到了这一点。我希望他们告诉过我。

chunks.text: Now, many people find that they are very disciplined about certain things. They're getting their sets and reps in. They're pushed past failure. They love their video games. They love perhaps mathematics, but not literature.
chunks.translation: 现在，许多人发现他们对某些事情非常自律。他们完成组数和次数。他们被推过失败。他们喜欢电子游戏。他们可能喜欢数学，但不喜欢文学。

chunks.text: The things that we are not facile in, that don't come easy to us. There're two reasons to do some of that learning at >> >> at every stage of life. One is it enriches us. We often find that the things that are hardest to learn, that we then learn, are the most satisfying. This is the effort that precedes dopamine is far more reinforcing than when just dopamine comes in.
chunks.translation: 我们不擅长的事情，对我们来说不容易的事情。在人生的每个阶段 >> >> 进行一些这样的学习有两个原因。一是它丰富我们。我们经常发现，最难学但然后我们学会的东西，是最令人满足的。这是先于多巴胺的努力，比仅仅多巴胺到来要强化得多。

chunks.text: You could say, "Well, you know, scrolling there's no um uh you know, there's no effort involved." And that seems very reinforcing. That's more of a compulsive behavior after a certain point. That's going to get passed into reflex. But, talk to anybody, anyone, and their life experience, if they've had a life, will say something like, "Oh, yeah, everything was going great until this big thing. Then I overcame that big thing, and that was really the thing that taught me that I'm capable of even bigger things, right?"
chunks.translation: 你可能会说，“嗯，你知道，刷手机没有嗯呃你知道，没有努力。”那似乎非常强化。在某种程度上那更像是一种强迫行为。那会变成反射。但是，和任何人交谈，任何有生活经验的人，如果他們有过生活，会说类似这样的话：“哦，是的，一切都很顺利，直到这件大事。然后我克服了那件大事，那真的是教会我我能做更大的事情的事情，对吧？”

chunks.text: I mean, no we don't really like success stories. We like um we like underdog often to success story, pitfall, come out of that. The hero's journey is something that we resonate with in part because it's so true, but in part because for so many people it's not true. We know it's there, but most most people don't embark on those things. And I think it's because we set too lofty an idea what the hero's journey is.
chunks.translation: 我的意思是，不，我们并不真的喜欢成功故事。我们喜欢嗯我们喜欢弱者往往成功的故事，陷阱，从中走出来。英雄之旅是我们共鸣的东西，部分因为它是如此真实，但部分因为对许多人来说它不是真的。我们知道它在那里，但大多数大多数人没有踏上那些事情。我认为这是因为我们对英雄之旅设定了太崇高的想法。

chunks.text: I mean, for a lot of people it's about learning to do less. I know a lot of hard driving people. It's about learning how to achieve more peace. It's about exploring ideas around spirituality or fiction if they only read non-fiction. I mean, we all have to ask ourselves how much should we push ourselves to do things that are that we're not just naturally inclined to do. I think a mixture of what we love to do and some of the things that we've just avoided because um they just seem too hard. I think there's real value in doing those things.
chunks.translation: 我的意思是，对很多人来说，这是关于学会少做。我认识很多拼命的人。这是关于学会如何获得更多平静。这是关于探索灵性或小说的想法，如果他们只读非小说。我的意思是，我们都必须问自己，我们应该在多大程度上推动自己去做那些我们并非天生倾向做的事情。我认为混合我们喜欢做的事情和一些我们只是避免的事情，因为嗯它们似乎太难了。我认为做那些事情有真正的价值。

chunks.text: And all the data on cognitive and maintaining cognitive ability say will exercise make you smarter? No. It's necessary but not sufficient to make you smarter. You still have to go learn. >> >> And it without completely joking, I mean this is evidenced by many guys that spend hours upon hours in the gym and they're not brilliant people.
